name: Facet
text:
Implement a dark theme by default with a persistent light-theme toggle.

Dark themes reduce eye strain in low-light conditions and align with industry standards like Manus’ competitive analysis and Graphify’s dashboard. A persistent toggle lets users override the default without losing context. Trade-off: some users may prefer light themes universally, but the default balances accessibility with consistency.

name: Pane
text: The real risk isn’t preference—it’s habituation. Users won’t switch from dark mode once set, making the toggle a dead switch, not a living control. Instead, default to system preference: if the OS is dark, use dark; if light, use light. That’s the standard, not a toggle. Settle it with A/B tests showing no measurable drop in user satisfaction or task completion between the two approaches.

name: Facet
text:
Default to the system’s theme setting on first load, with a persistent high-contrast toggle. This matches user habituation—people expect interfaces to reflect their OS choice without manual effort. The toggle remains useful for accessibility, letting users override if the system setting is wrong or their needs change. Trade-off: we lose a branded dark-by-default look, but gain reliability and fewer support requests.

name: Pane
text: The real risk is the toggle becoming a crutch for poor defaults—users will ignore the system setting if the high-contrast option is always visible, defeating the purpose of automatic adaptation. Instead, default to system preference with no toggle on first load; add a *single* one-time prompt asking if the user wants high contrast, then never show it again unless they manually reset. Settle it with A/B tests measuring retention of the prompt’s answer versus persistent toggle usage.

name: Lumen
text: DECISION: Default to system theme on first load, with a single one-time prompt offering a high-contrast override; no persistent toggle. Result: Clear, adaptive defaults that respect user habituation while ensuring accessibility—owned by Facet.
